abstract: A study is presented to investigate self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) models using physiological data obtained from non-invasive wearable sensors for mental stress assessment. The present work involved acquisition of electroencephalography (EEG) signals using wearable sensors, signal preprocessing, data augmentation, and investigation of self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) algorithms for multi-class mental stress assessment. Seven volunteers participated in this study executing various mental tasks while wearing an OpenBCI head cap to acquire EEG signals. The acquired EEG signals were preprocessed and utilized for data augmentation in time and frequency domains with different SSCL models. Optimal data augmentation combinations and SSCL models were identified leading to multi-class mental stress classification accuracy in the range of 98 to 99.9%. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of SSCL models using relatively small-size unlabeled EEG signals for multi-class mental stress assessment with a reasonably high accuracy. The potential of using SSCL models with EEG signals for mental stress assessment and intervention through human-robot interactions (HRI) is outlined

Stress is something all people experience, whether it is cognitive or physical stress. More people have reported to be suffering from mental (cognitive) stress in their daily lives in recent years. The coronavirus pandemic and the worldwide shutdown that was a result of it, have led to an increase in mental health issues and illnesses. A poll that was conducted at the behest of the American Psychological Association in 2020 showed that about 8 in 10 (78% to be exact) of adults who participated claimed that the pandemic caused an immense amount of stress in their lives, and 3 in 5 adults (60% exactly) claimed that the ongoing societal issues in America gave them a feeling of being overwhelmed (American Psychological Association, 2020). Occasional mental stress may not be considered damaging as compared to deadly diseases or physical trauma, but if persistent, can still have serious long-lasting effects on individuals.. Evidence from research has shown that long episodes of mental stress possibly lead to more significant risks of many kinds of health issues: cardiovascular disease, hypertension, decreased immunity, and possibly some forms of cancer (Cohen et al., 2007). Stress occurs in all organic life and is a complex natural phenomenon, caused by a perceived or actual threat (the stressor), causing the autonomic nervous system (ANS) to initiate the fight or flight response of the organism (Schneiderman et al., 2005). During the fight or flight response, the body of the organism diverts resources and energy from regulatory systems which are vital to maintaining the proper body functionality to physical and cognitive functions which are used to counter the stressor. The sudden shift of regulatory functions can manifest in a variety of responses to the stressor, such as changes in mood or behavior, fatigue or psychological damage, or a change 15  (increase or decrease) of physiological responses or signals (like future stressors) (Epel et al., 2018). A method or system used to detect stress levels and alleviate stress, if necessary, is needed to treat or avoid the adverse effects of stress on the human mind and body. Stress can appear as different forms of physiological and cognitive responses in the body. It is possible to measure the levels of signals and determine the severity of the stress (Sioni and Chittaro, 2015). Many methods can be used to detect and determine the level of stress, some of these methods being intrusive while others are not. A pacemaker or emission computed tomography (ECT) can produce accurate measurements of vital signs and brain wave activity, but these methods are invasive and could cause the patient harm and or discomfort, thus causing higher levels of stress. Thus, to cause little to no discomfort to the person experiencing stress, non-invasive wearable biosensors are considered ideal for detecting and measuring physiological signals to monitor the stress level in patients (Can et al., 2019; Sioni and Chittaro, 2015). These wearable devices are non-invasive and have the capability of measuring key physiological signals that are indicators of the wearer’s state of physical or mental stress. The most well-documented and common physiological signal measurement methods used for detecting stress levels include electrocardiogram (ECG), electroencephalogram (EEG), electromyogram (EMG), electrodermal activity (EDA), photoplethysmogram (PPG), galvanic skin response (GSR), skin temperature (ST or TEMP), heart rate (HR), and heart rate variability (HRV) (Can et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2018; Kushki et al., 2011; Liu and Du, 2018; Sano and Picard, 2013). With the extensive documentation on these physiologic markers, there are wearable non-invasive devices that can collect the physical and mental health data of the wearer. One such device is the OpenBCI Cyton and electrode cap. This device measures the EEG of the wearer’s brain at 8 different points at a sample frequency of 250 Hz (OpenBCI, n.d.-b, n.d.-a). 16  This device is readily available and easy to operate. The data is streamed to the connected computer (Sano and Picard, 2013; Thapliyal et al., 2017). The data collected cannot be easily interpreted by an untrained professional and is thus practically useless to the average person. In addition, there are thousands of data points collected every minute thus being too massive to sift through manually. To analyze the immense amount of complex data collected, many researchers have been implementing artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms in the form of neural networks to be able to interpret the data. Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are capable of processing vast amounts of numerical data all at once using machine learning techniques and mathematical models (Li and Liu, 2020). The ANNs are eventually able to make predictions of possible outcomes after being trained on sufficient data (Ghosh et al., 2022; Rabbani et al., 2022). Due to the learning methods used by different neural network models, it is difficult to know which model is the most optimal to use on different datasets. New and different models are being created, to choose from, but there are a lot of existing models that have extensive research and literature available on them that relate to mental stress only using a binary classification method based on the subjectively labeled data of the perceived levels of mental stress determined through a standard test in a laboratory setting (Can et al., 2019). The detection and classification of stress, both physical and mental, based on numerical data is a complex and thus a very time-consuming task.   1.2 Purpose of the Study The purpose of this study was to determine the best machine learning model that would yield the most accurate results when classifying and predicting levels of mental stress from relatively small-size unlabeled physiological signals. A requirement for this would be that the neural 17  network system employed needs to be able to analyze and organize datasets without the assistance of a human expert labeling the dataset (Saeed et al., 2021). The model employed must be able to analyze and cluster the unlabeled data free of human intervention. This can be achieved using a self-supervised learning model, particularly, a self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) model. Contrastive learning algorithms learn the features of datasets without the need for labels, grouping similar data points while recognizing the differences between the data clusters doing this through data augmentation. This process could increase the precision and accuracy of the data classification and predictions (Yèche et al., 2021). The performance of the contrastive learning model depends directly on the types of structure (framework) and  neural network  (backbone) of the model.  1.3 Hypothesis A non-invasive wearable device that is capable of measuring and collecting physiological signals is a relatively simple and affordable data acquisition method. The effectiveness of data collection using non-invasive devices along with general research literature utilizing the same or similar devices to monitor and collect physiological data related to stress levels, can produce neural network models to recognize people in mental stress. This leads to the current hypothesis “If small-size unlabeled physiological signals from non-invasive wearable sensors are acquired, then an optimal data augmentation combination along with a self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) model with multi-class classification capabilities can detect and predict mental stress levels of the wearer from the acquired physiological signals”. Objectives needed to test the proposed hypothesis are presented in the next section.  18  1.4 Overall Objectives and Scope of Research This research is a part of a greater project called Wearable sensors Assisted Robotics for Mental Stress (WARMS) in the Bio-Inspired Robotics and Intelligent Systems (B-IRIS) Laboratory under the supervision of Dr. Biswanath Samanta. WARMS is being developed as an automated system that can collect physiological signals from non-invasive wearable sensors and cluster those data to make distinctive classifications of stress levels. These stress level classifications will then be forwarded to autonomous robots that will carry out friendly intervention to reduce the stress levels of those wearing the sensors. The system will consist of an artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm to create a self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) model capable of analyzing and classifying the different trends and features in the physiological data. The protocols used to transfer data from the host machine to the autonomous robots will be a TCP/IP connection, creating a seamless human-robot interaction (HRI). The objectives of this research are: • Collect physiological response signals related to stress of varying levels using non-invasive wearable sensors to create a dataset, • Develop and train an SSCL model along with an optimal data augmentation combination for multi-class classification and prediction of stress levels using a relatively small-size unlabeled dataset. The following tasks were planned to achieve the research objectives: • Use a non-invasive wearable device like OpenBCI head cap to collect EEG signals from participants completing a series of mental tasks at different perceived stress levels, • Preprocess the datasets prior to data augmentation, 19  • Based on empirical studies of a group of SSCL models and data augmentation, select the best performing SSCL model and data augmentation combination for multi-class mental stress assessment.  1.5 Originality of Research and Potential Uses This research is distinct from others involving neural networks in that it utilizes a self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) algorithm with addition of a multi-class classification function within the network. Many studies focusing on SSCL models only implement a two-class (binary) classification function. By creating a contrast learning model that can divide the dataset into more than two class identifiers, the accuracy of correctly classifying unlabeled data increases and provides a more accurate representation of the values in the dataset correlated with the stress level of the subject. If the neural network can accurately classify the physiological data at varying levels of stress at a near-perfect precision, this could be a tool to help provide people suffering from stress with greater and more specific treatment options. The key points for the originality are: • Creating a self-supervised model that uses contrastive learning to classify physiological stress responses using relatively small-size unlabeled datasets. • Applying multi-level classification to identify stress levels with high accuracy.  1.6 Thesis Organization The rest of the thesis is organized as follows. These physiologic signals are involuntary responses controlled by the Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) due to exposure to external stimuli. The ANS is further divided into the Sympathetic Nervous System (SNS) and the Parasympathetic Nervous System (PNS), which control the galvanic skin response (GSR), heart rate variability (HRV), and brain wave activity (Chen et al., 2017; Jänig and McLachlan, 1992; Sharma and Gedeon, 2012).  Electroencephalography (EEG) is an electrophysiological process that records the changes in the electrical activity of the brain. Changes in the electrical activity in the brain describe the voltage changes caused by ionic currents within the brain cells. EEG activity is expressed as several types of frequencies and categorized into different brain wave signals. As illustrated in Fig. 2.1, brain waves can be categorized as Gamma waves (25 Hz – 140 Hz), Beta waves (14 Hz - 30 Hz), Alpha waves (7 – 13 Hz), Theta waves (4 – 7 Hz), and Delta waves (0 – 4 Hz) (Jun and Smitha, 2016). When the brain experiences stress, it is seen as a low-amplitude beta wave signal. The difference in frequency between beta and alpha waves can be used to detect stress.  23   Figure 2.1 EEG Waves in Time Series Graph (ItsuSync, n.d.)  2.2 Wearable devices  Cinaz et al. (Cinaz et al., 2013) ran a study investigating workload levels in office scenarios by first establishing baselines, then collecting data during a 1 hour of non-structured office workload, and a variety of classifiers were used with linear discriminant analysis (LDA) giving the best performance. Costin et al. (Costin et al., 2012)utilized morphological variability (MV) with HRV to get better HRV features. Ghaderi et al. (Ghaderi et al., 2016) used a database of sensor signals that were recorded from automobile drivers in Boston and selected best-in-class features per sensor based on their literature review, and classified driver stresses broken down to 100-second segments which had a 98% accuracy using the KNN (k-nearest neighbors) and the SVM (support vector machine) algorithm. The researchers stated that the respiratory signal was the most discriminative signal for classifying stress levels. Keshan et al. Gjoreski et al. (Gjoreski et al., 2015) used a dataset created by an app used by university students on campus to attempt to classify stress levels using exclusively smartphone-based features. The study found that smartphone-based features are not the best in class to determine stress levels. The study continued research on the subject adding new features like voice analysis and social media analysis to improve the rates of classification. Garcia-Ceja et al. (Garcia-Ceja et al., 2016) attempted to detect stress through the exclusive use of a smartphone accelerometer. They created a new technique to estimate heart activity based on the facial cues recorded 25  along with eye motions, mouth activity, and monitoring other facial features and were able to classify stress with an accuracy of over 91%.  2.3 Machine Learning AI is a term that has existed since the last half century and was first mentioned at a computer science conference at Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire. The initial objective of AI when it was first introduced was to model the human brain to create a more advanced computer (Lalitha, 2021). Machine learning is a subdivision of AI describing algorithms that can learn from previous experience (data) without the need for reprogramming. The algorithm can discover patterns from new data without the aid of human intervention. The program can achieve this by using algorithms that can learn from data by repeating the process continuously.  Figure 2.2 AI Structure Diagram (Mattab, 2019) In researching AI, computer scientists have made great progress in understanding what factors are needed to create truly intelligent machines which are: learning natural language processing and creativity. The two primary methods for creating AI were made: machine learning (ML) and 26  deep learning (DL). Machine learning is a subdivision of AI that focuses on teaching algorithms how to learn from previous data (experience) and make predictions from new data without programming a peculiar task. The hierarchy of AI is presented in Fig. 2.2 Machine learning can be divided into three major categories- supervised learning, self-supervised learning, and unsupervised learning. In supervised learning labeled datasets are used to train algorithms for classifying data or predicting outcomes accurately. This works by taking in input data that is fed into the model and adjusting the weights in the model until it has been fitted appropriately, which happens as a part of the cross-validation process. Some examples of supervised learning are Bayesian Networks, Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, Random Forests, Support Vector Machines, K nearest Neighbor, and Artificial Neural Networks.  2.4 Neural Networks and Deep Learning Neural networks are known as artificial neural networks (ANNs) or simulated neural networks (SNNs). This is a subdivision of machine learning. The mathematical structure of these is modeled roughly around the human brain, simulating the way neurons send signals to each other. The network consists of node layers with an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Each node is linked to another and has a defined weight and threshold value. If an individual node's output exceeds the threshold value, it is activated. This node will then send data to the subsequent node tier in the network (IBM Data and AI Team, 2023). Layers are linked together, with the output of one layer becoming the input of the next as seen in Fig. 2.3. 27   Figure 2.3 Neural Network Structure Diagram (Ognjanovski, 2019) Neural networks are trained to identify patterns in datasets using inputs from sensors or data streams. Learning techniques in neural networks are specifically developed to solve complex mathematical problems requiring vector equations and massive matrices. Training neural networks leads to improved efficiency and accuracy in data clustering and classification. Deep learning, often known as deep neural networks, is a subclass of neural networks that stack numerous node layers on top of one another. This is expected to improve the accuracy of the AI model. Unfortunately, by a significant margin, this makes the AI model computationally intensive requiring multiple layers and enormous number of labeled datasets. The weights assigned to the nodes inside each layer indicate the relevance of the corresponding attributes. Deep learning neural networks train on distinct attributes based on the input data from previous layers. The deep learning neural network features become more complicated as the data progresses through more levels. This architecture enables deep learning to manage enormous volumes of high-dimensional labeled data by utilizing millions of trainable parameters generated by nonlinear functions. The ability of neural networks to identify structures in datasets in both 28  real and latent space is one of their most important characteristics. This algorithm is not successful with high dimensional datasets because it is not feasible with large networks based on terms of time and space. Naïve Bayes (NB) is a Bayesian Network that has only one parent and several children with a strong assumption of independence among child nodes (Singh et al., 2016). This type of classifier converges faster than discriminative models and takes less time for training. NB has no free parameters to be set which simplifies it compared to ANNs and SVMs. Logistic Regression is a statistical model in which a logistic curve is fitted to a specific dataset, and this is applied when the dependent or target variable is dichotomous. This algorithm, unlike Decision Trees or Support Vector Machines, is good probabilistic interpretation, and the model can be updated 29  easily to take new data. This algorithm requires large datasets to achieve stable results. Decision Tree (DT) is an algorithm that uses the divide and conquer approach. This algorithm can handle a variety of data that may have missing values. DT is robust to noise, has a good generalization ability with redundant attributes, and provides high performance for a small computational effort. This algorithm cannot handle high-dimensional data (Singh et al., 2016). Random Forest (RF) is a collection method that operates by training multiple decision trees and returning the class with the majority of all the trees in the collective. This algorithm is fast, scalable, and robust to noise, however as the number of trees increases the algorithm becomes slower for real-time predictions (Singh et al., 2016). Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithms are complex but provide high accuracy. This algorithm analyzes data for classification and regression analysis. This model with an appropriate kernel can work well even if the data is not linearly separable in base feature space. The performance and accuracy of the algorithm are independent of the size of the data but are dependent on the number of training cycles (Singh et al., 2016). K Nearest Neighbor (KNN) is a non-parametric classification algorithm. This assigns to an unlabeled sample point, the class of the nearest of a set of previously labeled points. This model is suited for multi-modal classes as well as applications where objects can have many labels (Singh et al., 2016). Neural Networks are computational devices that are based loosely on the neuronal structure, processing method, and learning ability of a human brain, but done on a much smaller scale. This applies to problems where the relationships in the data may be non-linear or dynamic. Neural Networks allow for quick and relatively easy modeling of phenomena. Some variants include Deep Neural Networks, Back Propagation Neural Networks, Probabilistic Neural Networks, Radial Basis Function Neural Networks, and Complementary Neural Networks (Singh et al., 2016).  30  2.4.2 Unsupervised Learning Unsupervised learning algorithms take a set of data that only contains inputs and find the structure of the data by grouping or clustering data points. These algorithms identify commonalities in the data and respond based on the absence or presence of the determined commonalities in the new input data. An extension of the classic Random Forest technique, Unsupervised Random Forest (URF) is mostly applied to supervised learning problems. URF functions unsupervised, which means it doesn't need labeled data for training, in contrast to its supervised counterpart. Rather, it makes use of Random Forest principles to find structure and patterns in unlabeled datasets. In URF, splits are made according to feature randomness, and each decision tree in the ensemble is constructed independently. To maximize within-group similarity while decreasing between-group similarity, the algorithm divides the data into subgroups iteratively. URF is a technique that can be used to find hidden patterns, clusters, or anomalies in data by combining the output of several decision trees (Random Forest | Interactive Chaos, n.d.). Figure 2.5 Unsupervised Random Forest Structure (Random Forest | Interactive Chaos, n.d.)  31  2.4.3 Self-supervised Learning Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a type of machine learning, and in between supervised and unsupervised learning. This works based on an artificial neural network and the network learns in two steps. The task is solved based on pseudo labels that help to initialize the network weights. Next, the actual task is conducted using supervised or unsupervised learning.  An SSL model can educate itself to recognize or anticipate certain input elements based on other input elements. This learning strategy, which combines supervised work and unsupervised pretraining, is an intermediary approach between supervised and unsupervised learning. The supervised task is known as the downstream task (Td), and the pre-training phase is known as the upstream task (Tu). For the Tu, the model is trained on data with automatically created labels rather than ground truth labels. To enhance task performance and training, the Td initializes the algorithm using the neural network weights from the Tu (Rabbani et al., 2022). Using SSL has many benefits, including the ability to reuse the model for other activities inside the same domain. The model's ability to learn generalized features instead of task-specific ones makes this possible. When the model is trained for each task separately, it has been discovered to save computation time and enhance network performance. An additional benefit of using an SSL model is that it does not require pre-labeled data, meaning that bigger datasets can be utilized to train the model more effectively and build more complex networks (Sarkar and Etemad, 2022). This method has gained a lot of popularity in machine learning and has been applied in numerous recent studies since it can use more unlabeled data during training (Rabbani et al., 2022). A self-supervised multi-tasked learning framework for emotion recognition based on ECG data signals was presented in a recent study (Sarkar and Etemad, 2022). The suggested model is trained in two stages: first, it learns to recognize ECG representations, and second, it learns to categorize 32  emotional states. It was found that the SSL model in this investigation performed exceptionally well, achieving high F1 scores on every transformation. With an F1 score of 0.92 for the original signal and 0.93 for the scaling modification, the model was able to identify both signals. The SSL framework employed in the present research endeavor was inspired by  the model from (Sarkar and Etemad, 2022). SSL can be subdivided into generative self-supervised learning, contrastive self-supervised learning, and generative-contrastive (adversarial) self-supervised learning. Under generative learning, there are  Auto-regressive (AR) model, Flow-based model, Auto-encoding (AE) model, and hybrid generative models. AR models are Bayes net structures, and the objective of the AR model is to maximize the likelihood under forward autoregressive factorization. These models have been employed in computer vision. AR models can be applied to graph domain problems like graph generation. The advantage of the AR models is that they can model the context of dependency well, but a shortcoming of the model is the token at each position can only access context from one direction (Liu et al., 2021). Flow-based models have the goal of estimating high dimensional densities from data. The auto-encoding (AE) model can reconstruct inputs from corrupt inputs. AE models are flexible and due to this, it is the most popular generative model. Hybrid generative models combine the advantages of the AR and AE models. The autoencoder parameters are made to fit the auto-regressive constraints Click or tap here to enter text.. The advantage of generative models is that they can recover original data distributions without having assumptions for downstream tasks. A disadvantage of generative models is that when compared to contrastive learning models it is less competitive when classifying some scenarios (Liu et al., 2021). 33  Contrastive self-supervised learning creates different augmentations of the same input to have more similar depictions compared to the augmentations of different inputs. Some types of contrastive learning include Context-Instance Contrast, and Instance-Instance ContrastClick or tap here to enter text.. Context-instance contrast focuses on modeling the relationship between the features of a sample and the global context of the model. Context-instance contrast is further divided into Predict Relative Position (PRP) and Maximize Mutual Information (MI). PRP learns the relative positions of local components. MI focuses on learning direct relationships between local and global contexts and the relative positions are ignored. Instance-instance contrast learning discards MI and studies the relationship between different samples’ instance-level representation directlyClick or tap here to enter text.. The advantages of contrastive models are that they are lightweight compared to generative models because they discard the decoder in the algorithm architecture. Generative-Contrastive (Adversarial) self-supervised learning combines aspects of both generative and contrastive learning to maximize the advantages of both models though it still does have some drawbacks from both models (Liu et al., 2021). Artificial intelligence (AI), and clustering methods, allow medical researchers to discover new physiological relationships that have been previously undiscovered through traditional medical studies. This leads to finding new physiological relationships that can aid the derivation of stress levels possible. Physiological signals are high dimensional and complex, thus traditional clustering methods perform poorly (performance drops) because these methods perform best for simple data. Also, another issue that plagues traditional machine learning techniques is that they require feature extraction. However, this is not an inherent issue due to the fact there is no evidence that a signal set of physiological signal features correlates directly with stress levels and 34  thus a guessing game at best. An approach to classifying high-dimensional data is dimension reduction, which is possible through various methods. A traditional method of dimension reduction includes principal component analysis (PCA) (Wold et al., 1987), random forest algorithm (Breiman, 2001), and self-organizing maps (SOMs) (Kohonen, 1990). These methods could work great for some high dimensional data, but the high complexity of physiological signals often leads to mediocre performance using these methods. In this research field, Deep Learning has been the gold standard for dimension reduction as Deep Neural Networks (DNN) handle inherent non-linear relations well and eliminate the need for feature extractions. The combination of DNNs and traditional methods of dimension reduction has proven to increase the performance compared to the individual components (Xie et al., 2016). A thing to keep in mind is that the improper combination of DNNs and traditional methods of dimension reduction results in a performance reduction of the combination as compared to the individual components. DNNs need substantial amounts of data to achieve their optimal performance. A way to resolve the DNN performance issue is to use a probabilistic self-organizing map (PSOM). The method used to transform a self-organizing map (SOM) to PSOM is a cluster assignment hardening (CAH) method and has been proven to perform well in the latent space of variational auto-encoder (VAE) (Aljalbout et al., 2018). Fitting this PSOM into a VAE to train using combined losses has been proven to generate state-of-the-art clustering on high-dimensional, complex data (Manduchi et al., 2019). An advancement of this architecture by the same researchers was  integrating long short-term memory (LSTM) networks into the architecture to allow for time-series predictions (Manduchi et al., 2021). Using the modified architecture, the accuracies compared to the supervised machine learning techniques used for classifying stress could be achieved without human interference in the data labeling process and feature extraction. 35  2.4.4 Data Augmentation Data augmentation is a technique that uses pre-existing data to create modified copies of a dataset, hence artificially increasing the training dataset. This operates under the premise that, in a learned embedding state, distinct examples should be farther apart from one another, while comparable instances are closer together. The augmentation instances are encoded and projected into the embedding space before the CL objective is applied. The goal of CL approaches is to reduce the differences between negative pairs—instances from different samples—and maximize the similarities between positive pairs, or instances from the same samples. Through this procedure, the model is trained to maximize the distance between negative pairings in the embedding state and reduce the distance (usually quantified by a metric like cosine similarity or Euclidean distance) between positive pairs (Acharya et al., 2022; Qian et al., 2022). 37  Contrastive learning has gained popularity as a learning method and has been applied in several recent research, some of which focus on the recognition of emotions based on physiological data or human activity. Researchers suggest a CL model (Qian et al., 2022) that is perfect for small-scale human activity recognition (HAR) applications. The purpose of this study's model was to identify the optimal augmentation setup and technique to apply to datasets containing wearable-based data signals that lacked autogenerated labels. Two of the five proposed CL models—Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) and Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations (SimCLR)—were found to perform better than the other models in the publication. Additionally, convolutional neural networks, also termed as fully convolutional network (FCN), were found to be more resilient to HAR than other backbone networks.  2.5.1 Framework Models Many CL frameworks that had been previously established in literature were  utilized with modifications for the current study. These networks are effective at handling straightforward problems and can be used to extract features from more complex models. In contrast to data augmentations in contrastive learning, the backbone networks of machine learning models are typically less researched and are fixed to be ResNet in previously published works. It takes a solid foundation to learn representations in big datasets (Qian et al., 2022). This study analyzes six popular neural networks with representation learning that perform well with wearable data characteristics using a contrastive learning methodology. Transformer, autoencoder (AE), context autoencoder (CAE), fully convolutional network (FCN), long short-term memory (LSTM), and deep convolutional LSTM (DeepConvLSTM) are some of the popular backbone networks (Qian et al., 2022). It is mostly utilized for semantic segmentation. Reducing the number of denser layers in the network results in fewer parameters, which accelerates training. Typically, FCN is composed of an up-sampling path that facilitates localization and a down-sampling path that is used to extract and understand the context. Additionally, FCN uses skip connections to retrieve the fine-grained spatial information that was lost during the down-sampling process (Pathak et al., 2014; Shelhamer et al., 2017). An FCN backbone network is seen in Fig. 2.10.  43   Figure 2.10 FCN Backbone Network (Kodhai et al., 2020) FCNs can process images from beginning to end, which means they can take in a whole image and generate a pixel-by-pixel segmentation map. In contrast, conventional CNNs generate an output of a fixed size. FCNs use sampling techniques such as transposed convolutions or bilinear interpolation to recover the spatial information lost during convolutional processes, in contrast to typical CNNs that gradually degrade spatial resolution through pooling layers. This facilitates the creation of intricate segmentation maps. Skip connections are a common feature of FCNs that let the network use features at different scales. The accuracy of segmentation is increased by these skip connections, which fuse high-level characteristics (from later layers with richer semantic information) with low-level features (from early layers with fine spatial detail). FCNs are completely convolutional, therefore they can handle input images of any size. They are therefore more adaptable and appropriate for jobs where the input image dimensions could change. FCNs are practical for real-time applications because they are computationally efficient to train and assess due to their use of convolutional operations throughout the network instead of fully linked layers.  44  2.6 Multilayered Task Learning Multi-task learning (MTL) or classification is a machine learning technique where a model is trained to do numerous tasks at once. The sampling rate when using 8 channels is 250 Hz while when using 16 channels is 125 Hz. The Cyton board alone can handle 8 channels, but to collect 16 channel data the Daisy board is required to be added to the Cyton board. Using electrodes, the Cyton board's several channels—typically eight or sixteen—capture electrical signals from the scalp. These signals are tiny electrical potentials that the brain's neurons produce. According to the intended montage, electrodes are positioned on the subject's scalp in particular places (e.g., 10-20 system for EEG) (Electrode Arrangement According to the International 10/20 System, n.d.). The electrical activity produced by the brain's neurons is detected by the electrodes. The electrodes' unprocessed electrical signals are weak and prone to noise. The Cyton board applies filters to eliminate undesired noise, such as muscle artifacts and ambient interference and then amplifies these signals to make them more measurable. Analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) are used to transform analog signals into digital format following amplification and filtering. The signals are digitalized during this procedure, enabling digital systems to process them. After being digitalized, the Cyton board sends the signals to a computer or other device for additional processing and analysis. Usually, USB or Bluetooth connectivity is used for this. After the computer receives the data, it can be processed and examined using a variety of methods and algorithms. Filtering, feature extraction, artifact removal, and classification are possible methods to extract useful data about physiological signals, such as brain activity. Ultimately, the data that has been processed can either be saved for further study or shown in real-time. The findings can be interpreted by 47  scientists or medical professionals to learn more about patterns of brain activity, mental states, moods, or physical circumstances. The initial algorithm created to process data from wearables for human activity recognition (HAR) was changed to be applied to mental stress data for the present study. The University of California, Irvine HAR (UCIHAR) preprocessor code was a sub-algorithm from the original code that processed a dataset that was like the dataset utilized for the current study. This dataset is like the one made from the EEG datasets from the OpenBCI hardware (having 8 channels of data) in this study in terms of the number of feature extractions (UCIHAR has nine acceleration features). It was simple to include our preprocessed data in the CL model due to the similarities between the datasets generated for this study and the dataset utilized (Qian et al., 2022).  3.6.1 Framework Model: SimCLR While all the framework models from (Qian et al., 2022) were tested, the SimCLR framework was found to be the most reliable and was chosen to be the framework model for this study. SimCLR starts with an  unlabeled normalized EEG dataset. To augment this data, it applies a series of random transformations to each dataset in time and frequency domains which helps the model learn more robust representations. SimCLR uses a convolutional neural network (CNN), also termed as fully convolutional network (FCN), as its encoder. This FCN takes the augmented datasets as input and maps them to high-dimensional representations (embeddings) in a latent space. The key idea behind SimCLR is to encourage the model to map similar datasets close together in the embedding space while pushing dissimilar datasets apart. It does this by 62  maximizing agreement between different augmentations of the same dataset (positives) while minimizing agreement between the embeddings of different datasets (negatives). SimCLR uses a contrastive loss function, specifically the NT-Xent loss, to train the model. This loss function computes the similarity between pairs of embeddings and encourages the model to increase the similarity between positive pairs (augmentations of the same dataset) while decreasing the similarity between negative pairs (augmentations of different datasets). SimCLR incorporates two important components to improve the quality of learned representations: normalization and a projection head. Normalization (e.g., batch normalization) helps stabilize the training process, while the projection head projects the high-dimensional embeddings to a lower-dimensional space before computing similarities. This helps in capturing semantic information better. During training, SimCLR optimizes the encoder network parameters to minimize contrastive loss. This is typically done using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) or similar optimization algorithms. After training, the encoder network can be used as a feature extractor for downstream tasks such as dataset classification. The learned representations are expected to capture meaningful semantic information about the datasets, even though the model was trained without any explicit supervision (Chen et al., 2020). By making use of multilevel task classification to identify more than two levels of stress a lot of inconsistencies in the dataset can be cleared up to provide better results from the machine learning model. The multilevel task algorithm employed in this thesis is based on the method presented in the article (Sarkar and Etemad, 2022). In that publication, the researchers introduced a multi-task CNN model that learns by identifying various input signal modifications. The pretext job is represented by the notation (𝑋𝑗 , 𝑃𝑗), where 𝑃𝑗 is the automatically generated label based on the jth transformation and 𝑋𝑗 is the jth transformed signal. In this case, 𝑗 ∈ [0, 𝑁], where N is the total number of signal transformations. A signal transformation recognition network (𝑋𝑗, 𝑃𝑗 , 𝜃) is trained with a set of trainable parameters 𝜃 to learn the pretext task. By minimizing the total loss, Ltotal, which is made up of the weighted average of each loss of the signal transformation network Lj, the trainable parameters are discovered. All the objectives were accomplished in this research. Signals from the physiological data were gathered and preprocessed into useable datasets. The SSCL model was then applied to those datasets. This study produced an SSCL that demonstrated the ability to process several kinds of datasets and was able to classify different stress-levels. Determining the optimal configuration of the SSCL model and data augmentation for the assessment of mental stress was also critical to this research. Compared to alternative model configurations, the research showed that the SimCLR framework model with the FCN backbone network performed the best, with an accuracy score of over 99%. All data augmentation combinations had accuracy greater than 98%. The best data augmentation combination was found to be t_flip (to reverse the signal in the time domain) and ap_p (perturbation of signals in amplitude and phase) with an accuracy of 99.91%. The results of this research indicate that the data augmentations or training epochs have little to negligible effect on the accuracy of the models on this dataset, but these models have significant potential to differentiate among different stress levels. The accuracy of the URF model as compared to the contrastive learning model was significantly lower (92.31% as compared to 98.57% for the lowest CL model). The URF model had a significantly lower training and testing time (about 5 minutes) compared to the SSCL model (about 3 hours). The 90  HRI intervention of the robot was expected to decrease stress induced brain activity of a participant representing a decrease in stress.  5.2 Future Work The current study presented results using a limited number of participants. In the next phase the number and age group of volunteers participating in data acquisition are planned to be increased to investigate effects of the variability of acquired data and participants on the multi-class mental stress classification. The future scope of the work includes development of an automated system that collects the data from the participants, sends the data to a host computer for processing, assesses the mental stress level and based on the mental stress level above a threshold gives commands to a swarm of robots to act for reducing the stress levels of the participants. This is the overall goal of the Wearable sensors Assisted Robotics for Mental Stress (WARMS) project. The current system implemented for robotic actuation only worked with one robot and did not keep a real-time location of the test subject or the robot while moving. In the next phase it is planned to implement a system of collecting the position data of the robot and participants to reach locations near the affected participant. The system will need to be adapted to a multi-subject multi-robot system. Plans also exist to include facial recognition capabilities into the SSCL algorithm and HRI system to enhance communication and support for the wearer of the sensor. Lastly, there are plans to implement ChatGPT-4o into the HRI system which could enable real-time conversations with participants and help increase the overall stress reduction response and intelligence of the system.   91  REFERENCES Acharya, A., Sanghavi, S., Jing, L., Bhushanam, B., Choudhary, D., Rabbat, M., and Dhillon, I. 2022. abstract: In this thesis we will learn about what contrastive learning and time series are and understand the differences between supervised and self-supervised frameworks in machine learning. In addition, we will describe how the newest and most efficient self-supervised learning framework for visual representations to this date works, called SimCLR, which was originally developed to obtain useful vector representations from static images. We will also explain what TS2Vec is, and how a combination of both approaches can be applied to the concept of a time series, and still be able to extract a vector representation of the subject described by the time series, our goal is to show that even when the input dataset does not contain visual representations, contrastive learning can still be applied successfully, including when the whole subject data is spread between multiple time series

Master of Science (MS), May 2023, 34 pp., 3 tables, 11 figures, references, 31 titles.  In this thesis we will learn about what contrastive learning and time series are and understand the differences between supervised and self-supervised frameworks in machine learning. In addition, we will describe how the newest and most efficient self-supervised learning framework for visual representations to this date works, called SimCLR, which was originally developed to obtain useful vector representations from static images. We will also explain what TS2Vec is, and how a combination of both approaches can be applied to the concept of a time series, and still be able to extract a vector representation of the subject described by the time series, our goal is to show that even when the input dataset does not contain visual representations, contrastive learning can still be applied successfully, including when the whole subject data is spread between multiple time series.   iv  DEDICATION   I would not have been able to complete this master’s degree without the help of my friends, which motivated me to never give up my studies, and always pursue my goals no matter how hard the path might be to follow. Figure 11: Similarity Between Activities ......................................................................................29  1  CHAPTER I  INTRODUCTION   As time goes by, time series analytics[11] becomes increasingly important in all sorts of applications, since a time series is a collection of observations or measurements taken over a period of time (if you can imagine how a line graph looks, that is a good way to visualize how a time series looks like), this means that the more time passes, the more data we have to better analyze and study their changes over time, and therefore predict how it will behave in the future to effectively adjust for it[4][30], or sometimes identify patterns to react before a change occurs, maybe even prevent it entirely[14][30], this is particularly useful for many fields of study such as Finance[6], Medicine[9], weather forecasting[21], etc.   However, analyzing a time series can be very challenging for numerous reasons, the most important of them is to correctly extract meaning out of a time series [1][7][8], to do this a lot of context about the information is needed, we need to know the time period it took to get the data points, where the data was sampled from, and sometimes additional time series that were taken at the same time that together show the whole picture of what we are trying to study.   My goal in this experiment is to be able to apply an existing and very effective contrastive learning framework[5][22] to the concept of activity recognition within time series. Contrastive learning[17] is most popularly used to analyze and identify elements in images, and extract meaning out of the picture. 2  To have a computer learn an image representation has been a problem for many years, multiple methods have been proposed[3][10][15]throughout the years, and every time it’s getting better and better to the point where the results are difficult to optimize further as they have almost reached a hundred percent accuracy at identifying what’s inside the image, however doing this requires human supervision, it cannot be achieved without a lot of human power and time to reach high results. Numerous self-supervised methods have been proposed as well[12][20][31], but their performance was still far below their supervised counterparts, but everything changed when Chen et. al proposed a new framework this past 2020 during the pandemic. In their research paper “SimCLR: A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations”[5] they proposed a new way to teach a computer how to create a representation from an image that not only improves upon all previous self-supervised methods so far, but it can also get results up to par with fully supervised learning methods. Self-supervised learning applied in time series has recently become very popular as well[22][23][25], but in particular activity recognition[28] in time series has been an important topic of study with current emerging technologies. As years go by the internet of things keeps rapidly growing, and becoming more integrated in our daily routines, this means that devices that allow activity recognition in humans are starting to be present in our lives all the time, devices such as cellphones, smart watches, pedometers and more contain sensors and accelerometers that facilitate data gathering for a machine to learn about a person through these measurements captured by the devices. Activity recognition can be very important to monitor the health of a patient, maybe discover patterns that should be avoided, or even improve the general wellbeing of the user by preventing obesity or other conditions. 3  My objective is to be able to apply the SimCLR learning framework for a machine to be able to identify similar patterns within a time series, I will briefly explain how SimCLR works, along with how it can be applied together with a method to extract a vector representation from time series described in the research paper “TS2Vec: Towards Universal Representation of Time series”[30], as well as describing how it works. TS2Vec is a learning framework that is already very similar to SimCLR in the fact that it uses contrastive learning too, but their solution addresses the 3 main uses for time series analysis which are: classification (identifying the subject represented), forecasting (predicting how it will behave in the future), and anomaly detection (Identifying data points outside of what we are looking for).  Our contribution is to show how contrastive learning[17] can be applied for activity recognition[19][28] represented by time series, we use TS2Vec approach, but in contrast to the original application, in our experiments we are not trying to identify what the subject is, but we focus in identifying what activity is the subject performing at a given time, and successfully extract a vector representation of the activity even when the original data was fragmented. 4  CHAPTER II  CONTRASTIVE LEARNING  Before we talk about SimCLR, we first need to understand, what is contrastive learning? [17] This is when you take an image as a reference to use it as comparison with other images, and see how similar or different it is in contrast with the reference image. As a child you might have seen a puzzle like the one shown on “Fig. 1” this is an example of how contrastive learning can be used to teach a kid how to identify and sort out different objects on images by looking at the picture of the animal on the left side, identify it as a dog, and then search for a dog on the right side.  Figure 1: Match the animal. Puzzle designed for kids using contrastive learning. 5  As it turns out, this same concept used for a child can also be used to teach a machine to distinguish between similar and dissimilar things within images as well, in order to achieve this, the learning model for the machine requires at least 3 things to be able to solve this problem: A. Examples of similar and dissimilar images. In order to train the model, we need images that are similar to each other and images that are different, as shown on “Fig. 1”, usually in a fully supervised learning approach this part would be done by a human, they would manually pick images from a batch of files and label which images are similar, and which are different. B. Ability to know what an image represents. A mechanism is needed for the machine to compute the similarity between two images, even if it doesn’t know what the object in the image is, it should still be able to identify other objects that look alike. C. Ability to quantify if two images are similar. We need a method for the machine to compute the similarity of two images. It is important that it identifies that 2 images have some similarities between them, but we also need the machine to be able to tell how close of a match it is between the images. Why use SimCLR? The main advantage of self-supervised frameworks[20] is that they do not require human power to supervise the quality of the data, and label them appropriately. Supervised Learning[3] in comparison requires very large quantities of labelled data, but gathering good quality images and process them is a very time-consuming task to complete, and therefore very expensive as well, especially for something very complex as object detection, every time a new object will be 6  introduced to the framework the model has to be trained for it and data needs to be labelled again appropriately.  This self-supervised learning method[5] allows us to extract useful visual representations of the data using an unlabeled pool of images, making the process of gathering data much faster and because of this, even images that don’t have the best quality can still be used to contribute to mold the final representation obtained, including images where the object is not fully displayed. The reason to choose SimCLR[5] above all other self-supervised learning frameworks is the fact that in comparison with all others proposed so far[5][12][20][31], SimCLR is by far the better performing framework of all the existing ones, by itself the resulting representation models can be used to identify images with up to an 85% accuracy, but SimCLR also allows for the models to be fine-tuned after being trained, using a supervised framework with as low as just 1% of the data labelled to train the model obtained from SimCLR can increase the accuracy significantly reaching up to 95-98%, making the results comparable to those of fully supervised learning frameworks using a hundred times less labelled data. The only disadvantage of using this framework is that the computing power needed to be used at its maximum potential is enormous, the reason for this is that on each training iteration it uses a very large batch of images to process the similarity between them. In the recent years the availability of GPUs or TPUs is very limited because of the high demand they are hard to come by, and also very expensive, the original setup requires 16 GPU to be implemented the way it was initially proposed, but because of this limitation, I did not have access to such resources to test out the framework properly by ourselves, but we still implemented a simplified version of SimCLR to be able to run with just 1 GPU and test out its effectiveness. 7  How does SimCLR work? The algorithm starts by selecting a batch of images of a pre-defined size from the pool of unlabeled images collected, each of the images is then used for generating 2 augmented versions that had a random transformation function (refer to “Fig. 3”) applied to it as shown on “Fig. 2”, Xi and Xj are the 2 transformed images. Each of the generated images is then passed through an encoder f(.), this can be any generic encoder from the ones that have been proposed to this date, in the case of this project Resnet-50[16] is the encoder of choice, the result is a tensor representation of the images called hi and hj.  Figure 2: Simplified SimCLR framework. Original Image X is augmented by applying a random transformation to obtain Xi and Xj, these are processed through the encoder to obtain representation hi and hj, and then using a contrastive loss function through the projection head we get the final vectors Zi and Zj. Finally these tensor representations are processed through the projection head g(.), which is a neural network trained to maximize the agreement (similarity) between the two 8  representations using a contrastive loss function to calculate the similarity for all image representations, the final product are the final vector representations zi and zj , comparison between both final vectors is treated as a positive sample (similar images), and comparisons between one of the representations and the rest N-1 images in the batch (where N is the number of images in the batch) being treated as negative examples (dissimilar images). This process is then repeated for each of the images in the batch. Because the algorithm produces 2 augmented images for each picture in the data pool, this helps us create a larger data pool of 2N where N is the number of elements originally in the data pool. The negative pairs are not sampled explicitly, instead given a positive pair in the pool, we treat the other 2(N-1) examples as negative samples. The loss function used for a positive pair (i, j) is defined as: ℓ𝑖,𝑗 =  − logexp (𝑠𝑖𝑚(𝒵𝑖, 𝒵𝑗)/𝜏)∑ 𝕝[𝑘≠𝑖]exp (𝑠𝑖𝑚(𝒵𝑖, 𝒵𝑘)/𝜏)2𝑁𝑘=1   Where 𝕝[𝑘≠𝑖] ∈ {0,1}  is an indicator function evaluating to 1 iff k ≠ i and 𝜏 denotes a temperature parameter. The final loss is computed across all positive pairs, both (i, j) and (j, i), in a mini batch. 9   Figure 3: SimCLR augmentations. Examples of different transformations the algorithm uses to create augmented images, the augmentation transformation is chosen randomly. Besides these, the algorithm uses a few other transformations such as Gaussian blur, rotation (90, 180, 270 degrees), crop and resize. Augmentation The purpose of transforming the images is to help train the model to recognize the objects even when they are in different positions and look slightly different in some way, the resulting representations should be invariant. The image augmentations used include horizontal flip, a random crop of a certain size, color channel distortion, Gaussian blur, rotation in 90, 180, and 270 degrees, adding noise, etc. All these augmentations are designed to change the input image in a small way but not change the class of the image, as an example on “Fig. 3”, a dog would still be still a dog after flipping or cropping the image, and hence their resulting vector representations should not change much either, for the purposes of their experiments in the original paper the only transformations that were used were random crop with flip and resize, color distortion and Gaussian blur.  10   Conclusions  SimCLR is a great tool to extract useful representations out of images particularly useful for classifying what is the object within the image, the major advantage of this is that it can be done saving a lot of time gathering the data pool, as the algorithm does this from a pool of unlabeled images, manually labeling each image requires hours and hours of work, and because of this it is a very expensive task, besides saving time it also improves the accuracy by doubling the size of the data pool, since it creates 2 augmented images for each instance in the original data pool, and to get better results we need huge image pools to improve the accuracy of the machine’s performance to identify them. Because of the way it trains the machine, this solution is also very useful when gathering the pool of data in the first place, otherwise we would have to look for perfect reference image, but with this solution even incomplete images where the subject is not fully displayed can be contribute to the final representation, shortening the time required to gather a substantial data pool. Even though the original paper used it to obtain representations from static images, the same algorithm could be used to identify patterns in a time series, but the advantage that SimCLR could offer here is that in contrast to other existing methods to identify patterns in a time series, they usually rely in having a visual representation (a graph) created first and from there look for patterns, but the looks of a graph can change a lot depending on what is the timeframe used to create it, SimCLR could be able to identify the patterns analyzing the source data points directly, without having to obtain a visual reference first, even though the algorithm should be able to identify them that way too. 11   There are 2 major disadvantages for trying to implement SimCLR to process a time series, the first one is the way the data is presented, for SimCLR each image is an instance that it can analyze, each image already contains all the information it needs, but a time series is not always like that, sometimes the information is viewed from different perspectives and multiple time series end up forming the instance, another way a time series can be presented is by having a long time series that includes multiple instances at different times, SimCLR is not capable of identifying each individually it would take the whole timeline as one instance and that would make the final representation almost impossible to be accurate. The second issue are the transformations used for augmentations, because a time series is very different from an image, most of the transformations if not all of them introduced in the original paper are completely useless, cropping might be the one transformation that could still be used, but some major modifications have to happen to the transformations before they can be used for the purposes of this project. The opportunity to do fine tuning at the end might still be viable with a small pool of labeled data.12  CHAPTER III  TS2VEC  Most of existing learning frameworks for time series work by reading the data already divided into separated instances[1] (an array of smaller time series) or reading a long time series, and then figuring out a way to divide it into multiple sub-sequences[7] which would become the instances in that case.  TS2Vec[30] is a universal solution that can extract a vector representation of both types of input data, in addition TS2Vec can also produce a representation from an object seen from different points of view, for example a plane where you are tracking its change in speed and its change in altitude, two separate time series, but together they produce a final vector that better represents what the plane was experiencing.  Another advantage this framework has is the way contrastive learning is applied, TS2Vec operates using what they call “Hierarchical Contrasting” which applies contrastive learning in 2 major ways, the first is instance-wise which means it compares between different instances from the data pool, and the second is temporal dimensions which relates to comparisons between different segments of the same instance. In their original research paper “TS2Vec: Towards Universal Representation of Time Series”[30] showed that this framework generates great results when it was used for different tasks, primarily they focused on: Time Series Classification, 13  Forecasting, and anomaly detection. For the purposes of my experiment, I wanted to see if it could help for a different objective which is activity recognition. How does TS2Vec Work?  The first thing the algorithm does is sub dividing each time series from the pool into  collections of sub-series of pre-defined sizes, these would be the instances, each instance is then used to create 2 augmented versions of it by first phasing them out in specific ways, the first one has a small part of it left out at the beginning of the time series, and the second one has a small part of it left out at the end of it as shown on “Fig. 4”, doing it this way leaves a big section that has both of them overlapping, this would prevent the phasing from affecting the magnitude of the time series in general; the encoder is then used to process the overlapping section of both augmented series employing contextual consistency, the encoder has 3 components: an input projection layer, a timestamp masking module, and a dilated CNN module. The input projection layer is a fully connected layer in charge of mapping its observations at each timestamp to a high-dimensional latent vector, the reason to use a latent vector is to prevent the huge variance a raw value can have, raw values in a time series are unbound, and by using the vector we make sure the prediction of what the timestamp looks like under the mask is still within a certain boundary and this improves on the reconstruction of the section. The timestamp masking module oversees selecting random timestamps within the latent vector and masking it. This is also where the random cropping occurs, this helps to generate the augmented version. Finally, the dilated CNN module is applied to extract the contextual representation of each timestamp.          14   Figure 4: Simplified TS2Vec framework.Ttimestamp in red is used for one of the augmented representations, and timestamp in blue is used for the other, the middle overlapping section in purple is included in both red and blue timestamp, the encoder performs the transformations on the overlapping sections. Augmentation Since TS2Vec is not dealing with images, the augmentations it employs are different, and because of this they are also limited, Flips, Color, Blur and rotations are not options available for a time series, and even though warping is available, we have to be careful with this option because they could change the magnitude of the time series which could impact heavily on the information it’s trying to represent, for example a time series of a beating heart, if we warp it to make it look longer or shorter this can change dramatically what this could mean for the health of a patient. To overcome these issues, TS2Vec uses a new strategy named contextual consistency[8][25] to generate a positive pair by generating two augmented representations of 15  the same timestamp, the augmented contexts are generated applying 2 different transformations during the training phase:   Timestamp masking: Randomly masking certain timestamps of an instance, and then re-creating those missing sections to create an augmented context view of the instance.  Random cropping: Randomly cutting a small sample of two overlapping time segments. The reason these 2 were used is because both of them in conjunction do not affect the magnitude of the time series, since it was cropping sections that were overlapping, and the masked sections get re-constructed, in their original paper, timestamp masking was only applied when anomaly detection was involved. Visual representation of how the transformations are applied, the sections within the dotted line are cropped, and the sections with the question marks are the masks applied on top of them. Once the transformations are extracted, we use them for contrastive loss calculations, and as mentioned before hierarchical contrastive loss makes the encoder learn representations in different levels. Temporal contrastive loss takes the two augmented vector representations of a sample and treats those as a positive pair, very similar to SimCLR it then treats the rest of the 16  vector representations of different samples within the same time series as negative pairs. Their temporal contrastive loss function is defined as: ℓ𝑡𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑜(𝑖,𝑡)=  − logexp (𝒴𝑖,𝑡 ∙ 𝒵𝑖,𝑡)∑ (exp(𝒴𝑖,𝑡 ∙ 𝒵𝑖,𝑘) + 𝕝[𝑘≠𝑡] exp(𝒴𝑖,𝑡 ∙ 𝒵𝑖,𝑘)) 𝑘∈Ω  Where i is the index of the sample, t is the timestamp and Ω is the set of all timestamps within the overlap of the two augmented sub-series, and the two augmented representations are denoted by Yi,t and Zi,k. Instance-wise contrastive loss still uses the same positive pair from the augmented representations, but uses vector representations of other time series from the batch at the same timestamp t as negative samples, the loss function is defined as: ℓ𝑖𝑛𝑠𝑡(𝑖,𝑡)=  − logexp (𝒴𝑖,𝑡 ∙ 𝒵𝑖,𝑡)∑ (exp(𝒴𝑖,𝑡 ∙ 𝒵𝑗,𝑡) + 𝕝[𝑗≠𝑖] exp(𝒴𝑖,𝑡 ∙ 𝒵𝑗,𝑡))𝐵𝑗∈1 Where B represents the batch size. The two functions focus on different aspects of the time series, but they complement each other, while one focuses on the changes that occur in relation to all the time series in the data pool, the other focuses on how the subject in each series changes over time, giving us the overall loss function: ℒ𝑑𝑢𝑎𝑙 =  1𝑁𝑇 ∑ ∑(ℓ𝑡𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑜(𝑖,𝑡)+  ℓ𝑖𝑛𝑠𝑡(𝑖,𝑡))𝑡𝑖  After the representations are obtained, we end up with multiple representations of sub-series extracted from the main time series, at the end max pooling is performed on these groups of representations to get back the final representation of each whole time series. 17   Figure 6: Visualization of hierarchical contrastive loss. The section in green is a final vector representation of an instance, the final vector has the 2 augmentations overlapped and those are treated as a positive pair (denoted by the color green), while the rest of the instances are treated as negative pairs in relation to the green section, the horizontal axis in this example is where temporal contrast is performed, and the vertical axis is where Instance contrast is performed. Conclusions  TS2Vec performs extremely well when performing the 3 main tasks it was designed to analyze: forecasting[4], classification[14] and anomaly detection[18]. Time series classification is very useful to identify what subject is being represented, however for the purposes of our experiments we are looking to not only recognize what the subject is, but also what activity is the subject performing, the instance wise representations could be useful for this as they can help us recognize when the subject changes to a different activity in a long time series, this also tells us when it’s not performing any activity at all. Time series forecasting is one of the most used tasks for which these frameworks are created for in the first place, as it allows you to predict how a 18  subject is going to behave based on the observations of current data already collected about it, but another important use is that it can greatly improve the robustness of the data, if the data has missing segments at any point the prediction can re-construct the missing values making these instances useful, this is very similar to how SimCLR[5] also allows to use incomplete images as valid data entries. Finally time series anomaly detection is useful to identify if a certain section of the time series is an anomaly or not, based on the already learned representations of the subject, anomalies can cause the final vector representation to be less accurate as it could take them into account when training the model, but with this framework an anomaly can be either simply removed or be used to help determine when a subject changed from an activity to another, even if the new activity is not important (transition, idle, other activities outside of the study).  Even though both SimCLR[5] and TS2Vec[30] perform transformations their implementation is very distinct, while SimCLR takes the whole original image and transforms it to get the 2 augmented representation, and then process them at once to get the final vector, TS2Vec first divides the original time series into multiple smaller sub-series, and then transforms them to get the 2 augmented representations of each individual section to finally end up with a group of vectors that together represent the original time series. At the end to be able to get the final vector representation of the whole time series max pooling is performed to put the smaller instances back together, for both SimCLR and TS2Vec the loss function is applied at the end, but in the case of TS2Vec they added the extra step of performing max pooling right after.  TS2Vec has some similarities in their loss function to the one used on SimCLR, however the method in which it’s applied is also quite different, they both try to maximize the similarity between the augmentations, however because TS2Vec uses the hierarchical contrastive loss 19  function, the final vector has an extra dimension added to it, this is because the similarity is not only performed to compare between other time series in the data pool, but also to other instances within the same time series, another big advantage of using TS2Vec for our experiments is the fact that it’s able to accept time series with multiple features to extract valid representations out of them.20  CHAPTER IV  OUR CONTRIBUTION  Now that we understand how SimCLR and TS2Vec works, we need to figure out how this could be applied with the concept of activity recognition within a time series. A time series is when you track the changes in data over a period of time[11], the more data points you gather the clearer the series is. The first obstacle we can already identify is that even though you could visualize a time series (a line graph) the data we are using is not an image, SimCLR uses vector representations for the comparison, but we can’t apply the same method to obtain the representation of an image onto a time series. The data we are using for this experiment is the PAMAP2 Dataset[19], which contains data gathered using 3 IMUs (inertial measurement units) placed on the body of 9 different subjects (1 on the dominant arm wrist, 1 on the chest and 1 on the dominant leg ankle) and 1 heart rate monitor, each subject was recorded by these 4 sensors simultaneously, performing a variety of activities from a pool of 12 different activities for about an hour gathering more than 10 hours of information, about 8 of those hours contain valid information, the rest is information where the subject was performing transient activities such as: moving to a different location or idle while setting up the next activity, etc. Each subject has the information from all 4 sensors merged together in a single file which in total has 54 channels, the details of the information stored on each channel can be found in “Table 1”. abstract:
This paper presents Prototypical Contrastive Learning (PCL), an unsupervised
representation learning method that addresses the fundamental limitations of
instance-wise contrastive learning. PCL not only learns low-level features for
the task of instance discrimination, but more importantly, it implicitly
encodes semantic structures of the data into the learned embedding space.
Specifically, we introduce prototypes as latent variables to help find the
maximum-likelihood estimation of the network parameters in an
Expectation-Maximization framework. We iteratively perform E-step as finding
the distribution of prototypes via clustering and M-step as optimizing the
network via contrastive learning. We propose ProtoNCE loss, a generalized
version of the InfoNCE loss for contrastive learning, which encourages
representations to be closer to their assigned prototypes. PCL outperforms
state-of-the-art instance-wise contrastive learning methods on multiple
benchmarks with substantial improvement in low-resource transfer learning. Code
and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/salesforce/PCL
